ety.text: From Middle English hoppen, from Old English hoppian (“to hop, spring, leap, dance”), from Proto-West Germanic *huppōn, from Proto-Germanic *huppōną (“to hop”), from Proto-Indo-European *kewb- (“to bend, bow”). Cognate with Dutch hoppen (“to hop”), German hopfen, hoppen (“to hop”), Danish hoppe (“to hop, leap, jump”), Swedish hoppa (“to hop, leap, jump”), Icelandic hoppa (“to hop, skip”).

From Middle English hoppe, from Middle Dutch hoppe, from Old Dutch *hoppo, from Proto-Germanic *huppô, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *(s)keup (“tuft, hair of the head”), referring to the plant's appearance. Cognate with German Hopfen and French houblon.

senses.d: A short jump.
ex: The frog crossed the brook in three or four hops.

senses.d: A jump on one leg.
A short journey, especially in the case of air travel, one that takes place on a private plane.
A brief period of development or progress.
ex: For popular radio stars in New York and Los Angeles, it was a short hop to network television.

senses.d: A bounce, especially from the ground, of a thrown or batted ball.
A dance; a gathering for the purpose of dancing.
The sending of a data packet from one host to an adjacent host as part of its overall journey.
To jump a short distance.
To jump on one foot.
To be in state of energetic activity.
ex: Sorry, can't chat. Got to hop.
The sudden rush of customers had everyone in the shop hopping.

senses.d: To suddenly take a mode of transportation that one does not drive oneself, often surreptitiously.
ex: I hopped a plane over here as soon as I heard the news.
He was trying to hop a ride in an empty trailer headed north.

senses.d: To jump onto, or over
ex: They hop the curb and cut their engines.

senses.d: To move frequently from one place or situation to another similar one.
ex: We were party-hopping all weekend.
bar-hopping

senses.d: To go in a quick or sudden manner.
ex: Juliet shook her head as she hopped on the computer and greeted a customer who ambled in, blowing on her still wet nails.
Spangler hopped up from the control panel and stretched, pressing his hands to his lower back.

senses.d: To dance.
To walk lame; to limp.
ex: The limping smith […]hopping here and there, himself a jest[…]

senses.d: A plant of species Humulus lupulus, native to northern Europe, female flowers of which are used to flavour many types of beer during brewing.
The flowers of the hop plant, dried and used to brew beer.
Opium, or some other narcotic drug.
ex: ‘You've been shot full of hop and kept under it until you're as crazy as two waltzing mice.’

senses.d: The fruit of the dog rose; a hip.

ex: If you brew in March or October, and have hopped it for long keeping[…]

senses.d: To gather hops.
Synonym of half-op.

senses.d: To want (something) to happen, with a sense of expectation that it might [with that (+ clause); or (informal) with clause; or with so or (negative) not].
ex: They are hoping it does not rain, but I expect it will.
He's still hoping that everything will turn out fine.

senses.d: To intend to do something and look forward to the prospect of having done it [with to (+ infinitive)].
ex: I hope to succeed.
I hope to be going back again soon.

senses.d: To expect optimistically that one might get something (either a change in circumstance or an object) [with for].
ex: They're hoping for the best, but I don't think it's looking very good.
I'm hoping for my boss to offer me a pay raise.

senses.d: To place confidence; to trust with confident expectation of good [with in].
ex: I hope in thy word.
Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? Hope thou in God.

senses.d: To wish.
ex: I hope you all the best.

senses.d: The feeling of trust, confidence, belief or expectation that something wished for can or will happen.
ex: All hopes for a truce are gone after the latest attack.

senses.d: The actual thing wished for.
A person or thing that is a source of hope.
ex: We still have one hope left: my roommate might see the note I left on the table.

senses.d: The virtuous desire for future good.
ex: But now abideth faith, hope, love, these three; and the greatest of these is love.

senses.d: A hollow; a valley, especially the upper end of a narrow mountain valley when it is nearly encircled by smooth, green slopes; a combe.
